sections.title: Mission · Navigate the Linux Filesystem
paragraphs: Linux organizes data in a hierarchical filesystem. Learn to recognize files and directories, navigate, list contents, identify hidden entries and home directories, and distinguish absolute from relative paths.
sections.callout: KNOW WHERE YOU ARE AND HOW TO MOVE

sections.title: Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
paragraphs: Linux organizes files in a tree-like hierarchy. The filesystem root directory / is at the top, with directories such as /home, /etc, /usr, and /var branching beneath it.

sections.title: Exam Trap — Root Directory vs. Root User

table.caption: Same word, different concepts
rows: Root directory at the top of the filesystem

entries.title: Files
paragraphs: Files store data such as text, configuration, scripts, images, and executables. Linux does not require every file to have a familiar Windows-style extension.

entries.title: Directories
paragraphs: Directories contain filesystem entries such as files and other directories.
entries.memoryHook: Directory = container in the filesystem tree.

sections.title: ls
paragraphs: ls lists entries in the current directory.

sections.title: ls -l
paragraphs: ls -l produces a long listing with additional details.
sections.callout: ls = LIST · ls -l = LIST WITH DETAILS

sections.title: Hidden Files and Directories
paragraphs: Linux names beginning with a dot are normally hidden from ordinary listings, such as .bashrc. Hidden does not mean encrypted or protected; it is a naming convention.

sections.title: ls -a
paragraphs: ls -a displays all entries, including hidden files and directories.

sections.title: Exam Trap — Hidden Does Not Mean Secure
paragraphs: A dot file is merely omitted from ordinary listings. Permissions and security are separate concepts.
sections.callout: HIDDEN = NOT NORMALLY SHOWN · SECURITY = PERMISSIONS

sections.title: Combining ls Options
paragraphs: Commands can combine options. ls -la can show long-format details and hidden entries.

sections.title: Recursive Listings
paragraphs: A recursive listing descends into subdirectories. ls -R lists directory contents recursively rather than only one level.

sections.title: Current Directory · .
paragraphs: The symbol . means the current directory. ./script.sh refers to script.sh in the current directory.

sections.title: Parent Directory · ..
paragraphs: The symbol .. means the parent directory. cd .. moves one directory level upward.

sections.title: cd
paragraphs: cd means change directory. cd /home changes the shell's current working directory to /home.

sections.title: pwd · Print Working Directory
paragraphs: pwd displays the absolute path of your current working directory. Use it when you need to verify exactly where you are before or after navigation.

sections.title: Home Directory
paragraphs: Users normally have a home directory containing personal files and configuration. A common path is /home/username, although the exact path varies by account and system.

sections.title: Tilde · ~
paragraphs: In common shell usage, ~ represents the current user's home directory. cd ~ takes the user home.

sections.title: Absolute Paths
paragraphs: An absolute path specifies a location starting from filesystem root /. For example, /home/gsa/Documents/file.txt begins at root.

sections.title: Relative Paths
paragraphs: A relative path specifies a location from the current working directory. Documents/file.txt does not begin at root.
sections.callout: RELATIVE = START FROM WHERE I AM

sections.title: Exam Trap — Absolute vs. Relative Paths

table.caption: Identify the path's starting point
rows: Relative; starts from the current location

sections.callout: / FIRST = ABSOLUTE · NO / FIRST = USUALLY RELATIVE

sections.title: Moving Around
paragraphs: From /home/gsa, cd Documents uses a relative path, while cd /home/gsa/Documents uses an absolute path. Both can reach the same directory depending on the starting location.
sections.callout: THE CURRENT DIRECTORY DETERMINES RELATIVE PATHS
